cards.front: How do you explain window functions in a SQL interview?
cards.back: ‘Calculations across rows without collapsing them’: ROW_NUMBER/RANK for top-N per group, LAG/LEAD for period-over-period, running totals with ordered frames. The key contrast: GROUP BY collapses rows; windows keep row detail and add context.

cards.front: When do you reach for a CTE?
cards.back: Multi-step logic that reads top-to-bottom: each CTE is a named pipeline stage, chained like transforms. More readable than nested subqueries, and recursive CTEs (anchor + UNION ALL) handle hierarchies and date spines. The interview line: ‘CTEs are how I show my work.’

cards.front: How do you find ‘what’s missing’ in SQL?
cards.back: The anti-join: LEFT JOIN … WHERE right.key IS NULL, or NOT EXISTS (preferred — NULL-safe, unlike NOT IN). ‘Customers with no orders,’ ‘products never sold’ — this pattern is an interview staple.

cards.front: What does ‘aggregation at the right grain’ mean?
cards.back: GROUP BY must match the question’s unit: revenue per day vs per customer are different queries with different answers. State the grain explicitly (‘one row per customer-month’) before writing the query — interviewers score this discipline.

cards.front: How do you do set operations and conditional aggregation in SQL?
cards.back: UNION/INTERSECT/EXCEPT for set logic (UNION ALL when dupes are fine — faster, no dedup pass). Conditional aggregation — SUM(CASE WHEN …) — pivots and computes segment metrics in one pass. The interview line: ‘one scan, many answers.’

quiz.q: Putting a filter on an aggregated value in WHERE instead of HAVING is wrong because:
choices: WHERE runs before aggregation — aggregate filters belong in HAVING
quiz.explain: Logical query order: WHERE filters rows, GROUP BY aggregates, HAVING filters groups.

quiz.q: A sequential scan in EXPLAIN is a red flag when:
choices: It’s on a large table with a selective filter — a missing or unused index
quiz.explain: Full scans are fine for small tables; on large filtered tables they signal missing index support.

quiz.q: UNION ALL vs UNION differ in that:
choices: UNION ALL keeps duplicates and skips the dedup sort — faster when dupes are fine
quiz.explain: UNION’s implicit DISTINCT costs a sort; ALL avoids it when duplicates don’t matter.

quiz.q: COUNT(DISTINCT customer_id) vs COUNT(*) differ when:
choices: Rows aren’t unique per customer — COUNT(*) counts rows, COUNT(DISTINCT) counts customers
quiz.explain: Grain discipline: know what one row represents before choosing the aggregate.

cards.front: What pandas patterns must be muscle memory?
cards.back: groupby-agg-transform (split-apply-combine), merges with validated cardinality, pivots/melt for reshaping, and vectorized ops instead of row loops. The interview line: ‘I think in whole-DataFrame operations.’

cards.front: How do you handle files too big for memory in pandas?
cards.back: Chunked reading (chunksize) with incremental aggregation, dtype downcasting, reading only needed columns (usecols), or switching to a lazy engine (Polars/Dask/Spark). The interview line: ‘I never assume the data fits.’

cards.front: Why do datetimes and timezones cause interview bugs?
cards.back: Naive vs aware mixing, DST transitions (nonexistent/ambiguous times), and storing local time instead of UTC. The interview line: ‘store UTC, convert at display — and never do arithmetic on naive datetimes.’

cards.front: How do you handle nulls, duplicates, and type coercion?
cards.back: Profile first (missingness patterns, dup counts), decide per column (drop/impute/flag — never silently), dedupe on defined keys, and coerce types explicitly with errors='raise' thinking. The interview line: ‘every cleaning decision gets a reason, out loud.’

cards.front: Why do interviewers demand vectorized pandas?
cards.back: Row loops (iterrows) are Python-speed; vectorized ops run in C: groupby-transform, boolean masks, np.where, string methods. The performance gap is 10–100x — and the code is shorter. ‘No Python loops over rows’ is the rule.

quiz.q: Pure transform functions are testable because:
choices: Determinism: no mocks needed, every case is an input/output pair
quiz.explain: Purity removes the test setup tax; the function’s contract is its signature.

quiz.q: df['x'].apply(f) vs a vectorized equivalent: the difference is:
choices: apply still loops in Python; vectorized ops execute in compiled C — often 10-100x faster
quiz.explain: apply is a disguised Python loop; true vectorization pushes the loop into C.

quiz.q: Silent type coercion in pandas (e.g. mixed-type columns becoming object) is dangerous because:
choices: Downstream ops behave unexpectedly — a numeric column of strings sorts and sums wrong
quiz.explain: Object dtype hides the problem until an aggregation produces nonsense.

quiz.q: Storing timestamps in UTC (not local time) avoids:
choices: DST ambiguity — the same local time can occur twice or never
quiz.explain: UTC has no DST transitions; local-time arithmetic across a fall-back is ambiguous.

cards.front: Full vs incremental extraction — how do you choose?
cards.back: Full: simple, correct, expensive — fine for small dimensions. Incremental: extract since last watermark (updated_at, CDC) — cheap, but needs late-arrival handling and idempotent loads. The interview line: ‘incremental is an optimization with a correctness contract.’

cards.front: How do you discuss Airflow DAG design?
cards.back: DAGs as code: tasks are operators, dependencies define the graph, sensors wait on external state, retries with backoff handle transient failure, and SLA/alerting covers the on-call reality. The interview probes: idempotency (safe reruns) and backfill strategy.

cards.front: Spark: partitions, shuffles, and skew — the interview version?
cards.back: Partitions are the parallelism unit; shuffles (repartitioning data across the network) are the expensive operation; skew (one giant key) kills parallelism. Fixes: salting skewed keys, broadcast joins for small tables, and repartitioning deliberately.

cards.front: How do you explain idempotency to an interviewer?
cards.back: ‘Safe to retry’: repeating the request doesn’t change the outcome beyond the first application. Design it with idempotency keys on writes, and pair it with safe retries (exponential backoff + jitter) for distributed calls.

cards.front: What data-quality checks go inside a pipeline?
cards.back: Freshness (did it arrive?), volume (row counts in range?), schema (columns/types as expected?), distribution (nulls, dupes, outliers vs history). Fail the batch or quarantine it — never silently pass bad data to stakeholders.

quiz.q: A volume check catches:
choices: An upstream outage or partial extract — row counts far outside the expected band
quiz.explain: Row-count anomalies are the cheapest signal that something upstream broke.

quiz.q: An idempotency key on a payment endpoint protects against:
choices: Double-charging when the client retries a timed-out request
quiz.explain: The server recognizes the retried key and returns the original result instead of charging again.

quiz.q: Data skew hurts Spark because:
choices: One partition holds most data — straggler tasks bottleneck the stage
quiz.explain: Parallelism is only as fast as the slowest partition; skew serializes the job.

quiz.q: Airflow retries help with:
choices: Transient failures (flaky APIs, brief outages) — with backoff between attempts
quiz.explain: Retries assume the failure is temporary; deterministic bugs need a code fix, not retries.

notes.title: Sources
notes.body: - **Apache Kafka Documentation** (https://kafka.apache.org/documentation/) — Event streaming reference: topics, partitions, offsets, and delivery semantics.

cards.front: Event time vs processing time?
cards.back: Event time: when it happened (in the data). Processing time: when the system saw it (wall clock). Late/out-of-order data forces the distinction — watermarks bound how long you wait. The interview line: ‘processing time lies about the world; event time tells the truth late.’

cards.front: Offset vs cursor pagination: the interview-ready comparison?
cards.back: Offset is simple but skips/duplicates rows when data changes and gets slower deep into the list; cursor (keyset) pagination is stable and O(1)-ish per page using an indexed column. Choose cursor for feeds, offset for admin UIs.

cards.front: At-least-once vs exactly-once: the honest interview answer?
cards.back: At-least-once is the practical default (retries can duplicate); exactly-once needs idempotent consumers or transactions (Kafka EOS). The strong answer: ‘I design consumers idempotent, so duplicates are harmless — then at-least-once delivery is effectively exactly-once processing.’

cards.front: How do you handle watermarks, late data, and windowing?
cards.back: Windows (tumbling/sliding/session) bound aggregations in event time; watermarks declare lateness tolerance; late data past the watermark goes to a side output or triggers correction. The interview line: ‘every streaming aggregate is a bet about lateness.’

cards.front: Lambda vs Kappa?
cards.back: Lambda: batch + speed layers, serving merged (complex, battle-tested). Kappa: single streaming pipeline, reprocess by replaying the log (simpler, needs a replayable log like Kafka). The interview judgment: Kappa unless you can name why batch is required.

quiz.q: Kappa architecture simplifies Lambda by:
choices: Using one streaming pipeline with log replay instead of separate batch and speed layers
quiz.explain: If the log is replayable, reprocessing replaces the batch layer entirely.

quiz.q: Tumbling vs sliding windows differ in that:
choices: Tumbling windows don’t overlap; sliding windows overlap by the slide interval
quiz.explain: Overlap determines whether an event contributes to one window or many.

quiz.q: The most robust way to handle duplicate deliveries is:
choices: Preventing all duplicates in the broker
Idempotent consumers, so reprocessing is safe
quiz.explain: Duplicates are inevitable in distributed systems; idempotency makes them harmless.

quiz.q: Cursor pagination avoids the ‘missing rows’ problem of offset because:
choices: It pages relative to a stable key instead of a shifting row number
quiz.explain: New inserts shift offsets; a keyset cursor anchors to the last seen key, immune to shifts.

cards.front: What’s the STAR structure, and why does it work for behavioral rounds?
cards.back: Situation (2 sentences of context), Task (your responsibility), Action (what YOU did — the bulk), Result (measurable outcome + lesson). It works because interviewers score evidence of behavior, and STAR forces a complete evidence unit.

cards.front: Star vs snowflake?
cards.back: Star: denormalized dimensions (one join to facts — fast, simple). Snowflake: normalized dimensions (less redundancy, more joins). Analytics favors star for query simplicity; the interview follow-up is always ‘choose the grain first.’

cards.front: Slowly changing dimensions, types 1 and 2?
cards.back: Type 1: overwrite (history lost — fine for corrections). Type 2: new row per change with effective dates/current flag (history preserved — the analytics default). The interview question is always ‘do we need history?’ — that answer picks the type.

cards.front: Normalization vs denormalization in warehouse modeling?
cards.back: Normalize for write integrity (one fact, one place); denormalize dimensions for read simplicity (star schema). The interview line: ‘I normalize the facts, denormalize the dimensions — each for its reader.’

cards.front: What’s the bronze/silver/gold (medallion) pattern?
cards.back: Bronze: raw ingested data (immutable, append-only). Silver: cleaned, validated, conformed. Gold: aggregated, business-ready marts. Each layer has a contract; quality gates between layers stop bad data from flowing downstream.

quiz.q: dbt tests primarily assert:
choices: Data contracts — uniqueness, not-null, referential integrity on every model
quiz.explain: Tests turn assumptions about the data into verified guarantees on each run.

quiz.q: Data-quality checks belong:
choices: At layer boundaries — especially bronze→silver, so bad data never flows downstream
quiz.explain: Gates between medallion layers quarantine bad data where it’s cheapest to fix.

quiz.q: Star schemas denormalize dimensions because:
choices: Analytics queries read dimensions constantly — fewer joins, simpler queries, faster BI
quiz.explain: Read-optimized modeling: the query pattern (not write purity) rules the warehouse.

quiz.q: SCD Type 2 preserves history by:
choices: Adding a new dimension row per change with effective dates
quiz.explain: Versioned rows with date ranges: point-in-time analysis stays correct.

cards.front: How do you run a safe backfill?
cards.back: Idempotent stages, partition-scoped reruns (not full-table), throttled to protect production, validated against the original run’s metrics, with a runbook: what, why, scope, rollback. The interview line: ‘backfills are production changes with a plan.’

cards.front: How do you narrate design decisions aloud?
cards.back: Decision → alternatives considered → why this one (constraint it satisfies) → what would change your mind. The interview line: ‘I narrate the tradeoff, not just the choice — the reasoning is what’s being graded.’

cards.front: The interviewer asks you to go deep on 'End-to-end batch pipeline from raw files'. What answer structure makes you sound senior?
cards.back: Three beats: (1) one-sentence definition, (2) how it works mechanically, (3) when it fits and its key tradeoff — then stop and invite the follow-up. Structure is what separates a senior answer from a recitation.

cards.front: For 'Modeled warehouse layer with tested transforms', what’s the tradeoff question you should answer before the interviewer asks it?
cards.back: Every technique has a cost: name what you gain, what you pay, and when you’d choose the alternative. ‘It depends’ is only a good answer when you then explain what it depends on.

cards.front: How do you turn 'Data-quality gates and reconciliation checks' into a story the interviewer remembers?
cards.back: Anchor it to a decision: ‘we chose X over Y because…’ Interviewers probe decisions, not definitions — one concrete tradeoff you navigated beats three textbook paragraphs.

quiz.q: Narrating rejected alternatives is strong because:
choices: It proves you see the design space — choices are only meaningful against options
quiz.explain: A decision without visible alternatives looks like a guess; with them, it’s engineering.

quiz.q: Backfills must be partition-scoped because:
choices: Rerunning everything wastes cost and risks touching good data — scope to what’s wrong
quiz.explain: Surgical reruns: fix the affected range, leave correct history alone.

quiz.q: You’re asked about 'End-to-end batch pipeline from raw files' and your memory blanks. What’s the strongest recovery?
choices: State what you do know precisely, name the boundary, and reason from first principles aloud
Say ‘I don’t know’ and go silent
Change the subject to something you know
quiz.explain: Interviewers score honesty + reasoning: a precise partial answer with clear boundaries beats a confident fabrication every time.

quiz.q: The interviewer pushes back on your 'Modeled warehouse layer with tested transforms' answer. Best response?
choices: Defend your first answer at all costs
Steel-man their objection, check it against your reasoning aloud, and update or hold with evidence
quiz.explain: Pushback tests intellectual honesty: engage the objection seriously, reason aloud, and let evidence decide.

cards.front: How do you handle timed SQL rounds?
cards.back: The 15-minute playbook: clarify grain (1 min), sketch CTE stages aloud (2 min), write in passes, verify on a mental dataset, narrate throughout. The interview line: ‘method is the deliverable — the query is just evidence.’

cards.front: How do you handle framework whiteboard rounds?
cards.back: Narrate the architecture as you draw: components, lifecycles, data flow — then zoom into the probed area. The interview line: ‘I draw the system first so we both know where the deep dive lives.’

cards.front: How do you debug a broken pipeline in an interview?
cards.back: Narrow systematically: is it extraction, transform, or load? Check the stage’s contract (row counts, schema, DQ gates) — the failing contract names the culprit. The interview line: ‘pipelines fail at stage boundaries; I check the contracts.’

cards.front: How do you argue batch vs streaming tradeoffs?
cards.back: From the latency requirement: batch wins on simplicity, cost, and correctness-ease; streaming wins when minutes matter. Name both sides’ costs honestly. The interview line: ‘I argue from the requirement, not from enthusiasm.’

cards.front: How do you tell the data-incident story?
cards.back: STAR with data texture: the bad data, who consumed it, the blast radius, how you quarantined and fixed it, and the DQ gate you added so it can’t recur. The interview line: ‘every data incident ends with a gate.’

quiz.q: A redrill plan is effective when it is:
choices: Specific, dated, and tied to named misses from the scored review
quiz.explain: Specificity turns review into training; vague plans evaporate.

quiz.q: Ending with the added DQ gate is strong because:
choices: It proves systemic learning — the incident produced prevention, not just a fix
quiz.explain: Prevention is the deliverable; the fix was just the homework.

quiz.q: The deciding question in batch vs streaming is:
choices: ‘How fresh must the data be for the decision it serves?’ — latency need sets the architecture
quiz.explain: Freshness requirements are the only honest arbiter; everything else is preference.

quiz.q: Checking stage contracts (counts/schema) first works because:
choices: Each stage promises an output shape — the broken promise localizes the bug
quiz.explain: Contract violations pinpoint the stage; log-diving without them is wandering.

cards.front: Which distributions must you know cold, and when?
cards.back: Normal (means, CLT-backed inference), binomial (counts of yes/no), Poisson (event rates over time/space). The interview line: ‘I match the distribution to the data-generating process, not to habit.’

cards.front: How do you reason about expectation and variance in interviews?
cards.back: Expectation is linear (E[aX+bY] = aE[X]+bE[Y] — no independence needed); variance adds only for independent variables. Conditioning (E[X|Y]) is how you slice: the interview line is ‘condition on what you know, average over what you don’t.’

cards.front: Explain the central limit theorem plainly.
cards.back: Averages of many independent samples become approximately normal regardless of the underlying distribution — which is why confidence intervals and z-tests work on real data. The interview caveat: ‘independent’ and ‘enough samples’ are doing heavy lifting.

cards.front: How do you explain a confidence interval without mysticism?
cards.back: ‘If we repeated this procedure many times, ~95% of the intervals would contain the true value.’ It’s about the procedure’s long-run behavior, not ‘95% chance the truth is in this one.’ Wider interval = more uncertainty.

cards.front: What does a p-value actually say?
cards.back: The probability of seeing data this extreme if the null were true — NOT the probability the null is true, and not the size of the effect. The interview line: ‘p-values measure surprise under the null, nothing more.’

quiz.q: A 99%-accurate test for a 0.1%-prevalent disease: most positives are false because:
choices: Base rate: even 1% error on 99.9% healthy people swamps the true positives
quiz.explain: Bayes: P(disease|positive) depends on prevalence — rare conditions make false positives dominate.

quiz.q: p = 0.03 means:
choices: If the null were true, you’d see results this extreme 3% of the time
quiz.explain: It’s a conditional probability under the null — a common misreading is treating it as P(null is true).

quiz.q: A 95% confidence interval means:
choices: The procedure captures the true parameter in ~95% of repeated samples
quiz.explain: Frequentist intervals describe the method’s long-run coverage, not a probability about this interval.

quiz.q: The CLT justifies:
choices: Using normal-based confidence intervals on sample means from non-normal data (with enough samples)
quiz.explain: Sample means converge to normal as n grows — the foundation of classical inference on means.

cards.front: How do you make exploratory testing rigorous?
cards.back: Charters: time-boxed missions with a goal (‘explore checkout with invalid inputs for 45 minutes’), session notes, and debriefs. It’s skilled investigation, not random clicking — the charter makes it repeatable and reportable.

cards.front: What groupby patterns must be fluent?
cards.back: Aggregations (sum/mean/count per group), transforms (broadcast group stats back to rows), filters (keep groups meeting a condition), and multi-key groupbys. The interview line: ‘split-apply-combine is the grammar of exploratory analysis.’

cards.front: How do you merge without fan-out disasters?
cards.back: Check key uniqueness on both sides first (one-to-many is fine; many-to-many explodes). Validate with row-count assertions before/after, and use validate='m:1' in pandas to enforce expectations loudly.

cards.front: How do you handle missing and messy data?
cards.back: Diagnose the mechanism (MCAR/MAR/MNAR), then choose: drop (if MCAR and plentiful), impute (median/model — and record it), or flag with indicators. The interview line: ‘the missingness is data about the data-generating process.’

cards.front: What does good feature construction look like?
cards.back: Vectorized transforms expressing domain knowledge: ratios, time-since-event, rolling aggregates, encodings of categoricals — built in the pipeline (fit on train only) to avoid leakage. The interview line: ‘features are where domain knowledge becomes model power.’

quiz.q: Restart-and-run-all validates:
choices: That the notebook has no hidden out-of-order state — true top-to-bottom reproducibility
quiz.explain: Out-of-order execution hides state dependencies; a clean rerun proves the narrative is real.

quiz.q: Building features before the train/test split risks:
choices: Leakage — statistics from the test set contaminating training features
quiz.explain: Any transform that learns from data must be fit on train only, or evaluation is fiction.

quiz.q: Mean imputation’s hidden cost is:
choices: It shrinks variance and distorts relationships — the data looks more certain than it is
quiz.explain: Filling with the mean understates uncertainty; it’s a choice with consequences, not a default.

quiz.q: pd.merge(validate='m:1') is used to:
choices: Assert the merge keys have the expected uniqueness — failing loudly on fan-out
quiz.explain: Declaring expected cardinality turns silent row multiplication into a loud error.

cards.front: How do you discuss regression vs classification interview-style?
cards.back: Regression: predict a number (MSE/MAE, R² with caveats). Classification: predict a class (precision/recall, ROC-AUC, calibration when probabilities matter). The interview line: ‘I start from the decision the prediction serves, then pick the framing.’

cards.front: How do you explain overfitting and its fixes?
cards.back: The model memorizes noise: training error keeps dropping while validation error rises. Fixes: more data, regularization (L1/L2), simpler models, cross-validation for honest measurement, early stopping. The interview line: ‘the validation curve is the truth-teller.’

cards.front: Why three splits?
cards.back: Train: fit. Validation: choose models/hyperparameters (it becomes optimistic through selection). Test: one final unbiased estimate, touched once. The interview trap: tuning on the test set leaks — it’s just validation with extra steps.

cards.front: Precision vs recall — when does each matter?
cards.back: Precision: of flagged items, how many were right (false positives hurt — spam filters). Recall: of real items, how many were caught (false negatives hurt — fraud, disease). ROC-AUC summarizes the tradeoff across thresholds; PR curves are better for imbalanced data.

cards.front: What does feature-engineering judgment look like?
cards.back: Knowing which transforms encode real signal (domain ratios, temporal aggregations) vs noise-fitting, validating with ablations, and watching for leakage. The interview line: ‘a feature is a hypothesis — I test it like one.’

quiz.q: Naming what would change your mind is strong because:
choices: It proves the choice was reasoned — falsifiability is the mark of real judgment
quiz.explain: A choice you can’t unmake under evidence was never reasoned.

quiz.q: Ablation in feature engineering means:
choices: Removing a feature/group and measuring the performance drop — credit assignment
quiz.explain: Ablations prove a feature earns its keep instead of riding on correlated companions.

quiz.q: A fraud model needs high recall because:
choices: Missing fraud (false negatives) costs far more than false alarms
quiz.explain: The cost asymmetry decides: when misses are expensive, optimize recall and manage precision.

quiz.q: Tuning hyperparameters on the test set is wrong because:
choices: Repeated selection on the test set makes it optimistic — it’s no longer an unbiased estimate
quiz.explain: The test set must be touched once; every tuning decision on it leaks information into the estimate.

cards.front: Why is randomization ‘the whole game’ in experiments?
cards.back: Random assignment balances confounders — known and unknown — across arms, making the difference in outcomes attributable to the treatment. Without it, you’re comparing different populations and calling it an effect.

cards.front: What’s tickless idle, and why does power care?
cards.back: Instead of waking on every OS tick, the RTOS programs the next wakeup (timer or interrupt) and sleeps deeply until then — no periodic wakeups burning power. The interview line: ‘every avoided wakeup is battery life.’

cards.front: How do you read experiment results honestly?
cards.back: Check the primary metric’s confidence interval (not just the point estimate), verify guardrail metrics didn’t regress, look for heterogeneous effects across segments, and confirm the result survives the pre-registered analysis. The interview line: ‘I report what the data says, including the inconvenient parts.’

cards.front: Why is peeking at A/B results a sin?
cards.back: Every peek is another chance for noise to look significant — the false-positive rate compounds with each look. Fixes: pre-commit to runtime from power analysis, or use sequential methods designed for interim looks. The interview line: ‘decide the stopping rule before the test starts.’

cards.front: When do you NOT A/B test?
cards.back: When you can’t randomize cleanly (network effects, tiny samples), when the effect needs months to matter, when it’s unethical, or when the answer is obvious from data. Alternatives: quasi-experiments (diff-in-diff), holdouts, or just ship with monitoring.

quiz.q: Pre-registering the analysis plan prevents:
choices: HARKing — hypothesizing after results are known, and metric cherry-picking
quiz.explain: Decisions made after seeing data are rationalizations; pre-registration keeps the test honest.

quiz.q: Network effects (users influencing each other) break A/B tests because:
choices: Treatment leaks into control — randomization’s promise broken
quiz.explain: Randomization assumes independent units; interference between users contaminates both arms.

quiz.q: Peeking inflates false positives because:
choices: Each interim look is another roll of the dice — significance under repeated testing isn’t 5% anymore
quiz.explain: Multiple comparisons: with enough looks, noise will eventually cross the threshold.

quiz.q: A significant primary metric with regressed guardrail metrics means:
choices: The win has a cost — investigate the tradeoff before deciding
quiz.explain: Guardrails exist to catch wins that break something else; net impact decides.

cards.front: How do you frame an ambiguous business question?
cards.back: Restate it as a measurable question, choose metrics before touching data (what would change your mind?), then plan the analysis. The interview line: ‘metrics first, data second — otherwise the data picks the question for you.’

cards.front: What goes in an analysis plan, and what are sanity checks?
cards.back: Plan: question, metrics, data sources, methods, caveats — written before touching data. Sanity checks: row counts, distributions, known totals — run first, every time. The interview line: ‘the plan prevents fishing; the checks prevent embarrassment.’

cards.front: How do you build a case-study narrative?
cards.back: Arc: question → approach → key findings (one chart each) → recommendation. Anticipate follow-ups (caveats, alternative explanations) and address the biggest one proactively. The one-page summary: decision, evidence, risks — nothing else.

cards.front: The interviewer asks you to go deep on 'Framing an ambiguous business question'. What answer structure makes you sound senior?
cards.back: Three beats: (1) one-sentence definition, (2) how it works mechanically, (3) when it fits and its key tradeoff — then stop and invite the follow-up. Structure is what separates a senior answer from a recitation.

cards.front: For 'Choosing metrics before touching data', what’s the tradeoff question you should answer before the interviewer asks it?
cards.back: Every technique has a cost: name what you gain, what you pay, and when you’d choose the alternative. ‘It depends’ is only a good answer when you then explain what it depends on.

quiz.q: Addressing the biggest objection proactively is strong because:
choices: It shows you’ve stress-tested your own conclusion — credibility before they ask
quiz.explain: Pre-empting the obvious challenge proves the analysis survived contact with skepticism.

quiz.q: Sanity checks come before analysis because:
choices: Garbage in, garbage out — validating the data’s shape first saves the whole analysis
quiz.explain: An analysis on broken data is worse than no analysis — it’s confidently wrong.

quiz.q: Choosing metrics before touching data prevents:
choices: Confirmation bias — shopping for metrics that support a preferred answer
quiz.explain: Pre-committed metrics keep the analysis honest when the data disappoints.

quiz.q: You’re asked about 'Framing an ambiguous business question' and your memory blanks. What’s the strongest recovery?
choices: State what you do know precisely, name the boundary, and reason from first principles aloud
Say ‘I don’t know’ and go silent
Change the subject to something you know
quiz.explain: Interviewers score honesty + reasoning: a precise partial answer with clear boundaries beats a confident fabrication every time.

cards.front: What’s the logical order of a SQL query — and why does it matter?
cards.back: FROM → WHERE → GROUP BY → HAVING → SELECT → ORDER BY: the written order isn’t the execution order. It matters because aliases defined in SELECT aren’t visible in WHERE, and window functions come after WHERE — the interview line: ‘I write in SELECT order but think in execution order.’

cards.front: Inner vs left join — when does each lie?
cards.back: Inner drops non-matching rows from both sides (silently shrinking your denominator). Left keeps all left rows with NULLs for misses. The lie: inner-joining then counting ‘all users’ — you’ve excluded the unmatched. State which side must survive.

cards.front: What do GROUP BY mistakes look like in interviews?
cards.back: Selecting non-aggregated columns not in the GROUP BY (invalid or arbitrary), filtering groups in WHERE instead of HAVING, and wrong grain (grouping by day when the question wants per user). The interview line: ‘every SELECT column is either grouped or aggregated — no exceptions.’

cards.front: COUNT(*) vs COUNT(column)?
cards.back: COUNT(*) counts rows; COUNT(column) counts non-NULL values in that column. The interview trap: ‘how many users?’ with nullable columns — pick the wrong one and your metric is silently off.

cards.front: When do you use EXISTS vs a JOIN?
cards.back: EXISTS for semi-join questions (‘customers WITH orders’) — it stops at the first match and never fans out. JOIN when you need columns from the other table. The interview line: ‘EXISTS asks a yes/no question; JOIN brings back data.’

quiz.q: NOT IN is dangerous with NULLs because:
choices: A single NULL in the subquery makes the whole predicate UNKNOWN — zero rows returned
quiz.explain: NULL semantics: NOT IN with a NULL never evaluates true; NOT EXISTS doesn’t have this trap.

quiz.q: EXISTS is preferred over IN for ‘has at least one’ because:
choices: It short-circuits on first match and is NULL-safe
quiz.explain: Correlated EXISTS stops scanning at the first hit; IN materializes the whole set.

quiz.q: COUNT(email) < COUNT(*) means:
choices: Some rows have NULL email — COUNT(column) skips NULLs
quiz.explain: COUNT(column) excludes NULLs; COUNT(*) counts every row regardless.

quiz.q: Filtering on SUM(revenue) > 1000 belongs in:
choices: HAVING — it filters groups after aggregation
quiz.explain: WHERE filters rows pre-aggregation; HAVING filters the grouped results.

cards.front: Absolute vs relative references — the 30-second version?
cards.back: $ locks the reference: $A$1 never moves, A$1 locks the row, $A1 locks the column. The interview line: ‘I lock what shouldn’t move when the formula fills — getting this wrong is the #1 spreadsheet bug.’

cards.front: What are pivot tables for in an interview?
cards.back: Fast exploratory aggregation: drag dimensions to rows/columns, values to aggregation — distributions and cuts in seconds, no formulas. The interview line: ‘pivots are the spreadsheet’s GROUP BY.’

cards.front: What spreadsheet techniques do interviewers probe?

cards.front: When does a spreadsheet stop being the right tool?

quiz.q: Formula-based cleaning beats manual edits because:

quiz.q: A pivot table’s ‘values’ field with ‘count’ answers:

cards.back: A y-axis not starting at zero visually magnifies tiny differences — honest or sloppy, it misleads. The interview line: ‘I check the axis before I believe the chart — including my own.’

cards.front: What makes a dashboard that ‘answers questions’?
cards.back: Golden signals up top, drill-down from symptom to cause, time-range comparisons, and annotations for deploys — organized by the questions on-call asks at 3am, not by data source. The interview line: ‘a dashboard is a UI for incident questions.’

cards.front: What’s the insight → action → recommendation arc?
cards.back: Insight (what the data says), implication (why it matters to the business), recommendation (what to do, with expected impact). Data without a recommendation is trivia; the arc turns analysis into decisions.

cards.front: How do you present to non-technical stakeholders?
cards.back: Lead with the recommendation, then the one chart that proves it; plain language, no jargon; name caveats briefly and honestly; end with the decision you need. The interview line: ‘I present conclusions, not queries.’

quiz.q: The first critique question for any chart is:
choices: What question is it answering — and does the visual actually answer it
quiz.explain: A beautiful chart answering the wrong question is worse than no chart.

quiz.q: Leading with the recommendation works because:
choices: Executives decide — the supporting evidence follows the decision they need to make
quiz.explain: BLUF (bottom line up front): busy stakeholders need the ask before the analysis.

quiz.q: An analysis without a recommendation is weak because:
choices: Stakeholders need decisions, not trivia — the arc connects data to action
quiz.explain: The job is driving decisions; insight and implication earn the right to recommend.

quiz.q: Deploy annotations on dashboards help because:
choices: They correlate behavior changes with releases — the first suspect in any regression
quiz.explain: ‘What changed?’ is the first incident question; annotations answer it at a glance.

cards.front: What’s the STAR structure, and why does it work for behavioral rounds?
cards.back: Situation (2 sentences of context), Task (your responsibility), Action (what YOU did — the bulk), Result (measurable outcome + lesson). It works because interviewers score evidence of behavior, and STAR forces a complete evidence unit.

cards.front: How do you analyze a funnel?
cards.back: Step-by-step conversion with drop-off at each stage, segmented (device, cohort, channel) because aggregate funnels hide the story. The interview move: name the biggest absolute drop first — that’s where the leverage is.

cards.front: Cohorts and retention curves — the interview version?
cards.back: Group users by start period (cohort), track retention over time since start: the curve’s shape reveals product health (flattening = sticky, decaying to zero = leaky bucket). Compare cohorts to measure whether changes actually improved retention.

cards.front: Why segment before concluding?
cards.back: Aggregates lie (Simpson’s paradox): the overall trend can reverse within segments. The interview line: ‘I never trust an aggregate until I’ve cut it three ways.’

cards.front: How do you read an experiment result honestly?
cards.back: Primary metric’s confidence interval (not just the point), guardrails for regressions, segment heterogeneity, and whether the result survives the pre-registered analysis. The interview line: ‘I report what the data says, including the inconvenient parts.’

quiz.q: The FIRST step when a metric moves unexpectedly is:
choices: Verify data quality — instrumentation, pipeline, definitions
quiz.explain: Half of all ‘metric moves’ are measurement artifacts; rule those out before theorizing.

quiz.q: A significant primary metric with regressed guardrails means:
choices: The win has a cost — investigate the tradeoff before deciding
quiz.explain: Guardrails exist to catch wins that break something else; net impact decides.

quiz.q: Simpson’s paradox warns that:
choices: An aggregate trend can reverse within subgroups — always check segments
quiz.explain: A treatment can look better overall yet worse in every segment — composition effects deceive.

quiz.q: A retention curve flattening above zero indicates:
choices: A sticky core of users who stay — product-market fit signal
quiz.explain: Flattening means a fraction never leaves; decaying to zero means everyone eventually churns.

cards.back: Pick a question worth answering (decision attached), get and clean the data with auditable steps, explore with a plan, build the dashboard or deck around the insight-action arc, and write the recommendation memo anticipating pushback. The interview line: ‘every step serves the decision.’

cards.front: How do you make exploratory testing rigorous?
cards.back: Charters: time-boxed missions with a goal (‘explore checkout with invalid inputs for 45 minutes’), session notes, and debriefs. It’s skilled investigation, not random clicking — the charter makes it repeatable and reportable.

cards.front: memo, useMemo, useCallback — when is each the right call?
cards.back: memo: skip re-rendering a component when props are shallow-equal (for expensive subtrees). useMemo: cache an expensive computation. useCallback: stabilize a function identity passed to memoized children. And the caveat: don’t memoize everything — measure first.

cards.front: How do you handle stakeholder disagreement?

cards.front: The interviewer asks you to go deep on 'Picking a question worth answering'. What answer structure makes you sound senior?
cards.back: Three beats: (1) one-sentence definition, (2) how it works mechanically, (3) when it fits and its key tradeoff — then stop and invite the follow-up. Structure is what separates a senior answer from a recitation.

quiz.q: When a stakeholder rejects your analysis, the strongest first move is:
choices: Understand their objection — it’s often a different question than you answered
quiz.explain: Most ‘disagreements’ are misaligned questions; diagnosing the real one resolves them.

quiz.q: useCallback’s purpose is:
choices: Preserving function identity across renders so memoized children don’t re-render
quiz.explain: A new function identity each render defeats memo on children; useCallback stabilizes it.

quiz.q: An exploratory testing charter provides:
choices: A time-boxed mission and focus — making exploration deliberate and reportable
quiz.explain: Charters bound the session with purpose; notes and debriefs turn findings into artifacts.

quiz.q: Attaching a decision to the question upfront matters because:
choices: It scopes the analysis — you know when you have enough to recommend
quiz.explain: Decision-less analysis expands forever; a target decision bounds the work.

cards.front: Bias-variance tradeoff, precisely?
cards.back: Expected error = bias² + variance + irreducible noise. Simple models: high bias (underfit). Complex models: high variance (overfit). The sweet spot minimizes total error — found via validation curves, controlled with regularization, data, and model choice.

cards.front: L1 vs L2 regularization?
cards.back: L1 (lasso): penalizes |w| — drives weights to exactly zero (feature selection, sparse). L2 (ridge): penalizes w² — shrinks weights smoothly (handles correlated features). Elastic net combines both. The interview line: ‘L1 selects, L2 shrinks.’

cards.front: Maximum likelihood intuition?
cards.back: Choose the parameters that make the observed data most probable: maximize P(data|θ). Least squares IS MLE under Gaussian noise; cross-entropy IS MLE for classification. The interview line: ‘most loss functions are MLE in disguise.’

cards.front: Gradient descent variants and failure modes?
cards.back: Batch (exact, slow), SGD (noisy, fast, escapes shallow minima), mini-batch (the practical default). Failure modes: too-large lr diverges, too-small crawls, ravines need momentum/Adam, saddle points slow progress. The interview line: ‘lr is the most important hyperparameter.’

cards.front: How do you discuss decision boundaries of common models?
cards.back: Logistic regression: linear. Trees: axis-aligned rectangles. SVM (RBF): smooth nonlinear. kNN: Voronoi-ish local. Neural nets: learned hierarchical. The interview line: ‘the boundary shape tells you the model’s inductive bias.’

quiz.q: Deriving on the whiteboard is stronger than reciting because:
choices: It proves understanding — and lets you recover when memory fails mid-step
quiz.explain: Derivations are checkable reasoning; recitation is untestable until it breaks.

quiz.q: A single decision tree’s boundary is:
choices: Axis-aligned rectangles — splits are one feature at a time
quiz.explain: Each split thresholds one feature: the boundary is a union of boxes.

quiz.q: Diverging loss (NaN/inf) in training most likely means:
choices: Learning rate too large for the loss curvature
quiz.explain: Overshooting the minimum repeatedly: reduce lr (or add scheduling/clipping) first.

quiz.q: Minimizing MSE is equivalent to MLE under:
quiz.explain: The Gaussian likelihood’s log is the squared error (up to constants) — same optimum.

cards.front: Backprop in one breath?
cards.back: The chain rule applied to the computation graph: forward pass computes values, backward pass propagates gradients from loss to parameters via local derivatives. That’s it — every deep learning framework is chain rule + bookkeeping.

cards.front: Why do activations and initialization matter?
cards.back: Without nonlinear activations, deep nets collapse to linear models. ReLU (and variants) is the default: cheap, avoids saturation. Initialization (He/Xavier) keeps signal/variance stable across layers — bad init means vanishing/exploding gradients before training starts.

cards.front: Why do convolutions fit images?
cards.back: Local connectivity + weight sharing: filters detect local patterns (edges → textures → objects) anywhere in the image, with far fewer parameters than dense layers. Translation equivariance: a cat is a cat wherever it appears.

cards.front: RNNs, LSTMs, and the attention handoff?
cards.back: RNNs: sequential, vanishing gradients over long sequences. LSTMs: gates preserve long-term state — better, still sequential. Attention: all-pairs interactions in parallel, no recurrence — the handoff that enabled transformers. The interview line: ‘attention replaced recurrence because parallelism won.’

cards.front: How do you fight overfitting in deep nets?
cards.back: Dropout (randomly zero activations — trains an ensemble of subnetworks), weight decay, data augmentation, early stopping on validation, and batch/layer norm stabilizing training. The interview line: ‘regularization is how I spend my variance budget.’

quiz.q: Training loss falling while validation loss rises means:
choices: Overfitting — the model memorizes training noise
quiz.explain: The divergence point is where generalization ends; early stopping lives there.

quiz.q: Dropout at training time:
choices: Randomly zeroes activations so the network can’t rely on any single unit — an implicit ensemble
quiz.explain: Forcing redundancy across units prevents co-adaptation; at inference the full network is used (scaled).

quiz.q: Attention’s decisive advantage over RNNs is:
choices: Parallel computation across the sequence — no sequential bottleneck
quiz.explain: RNNs process tokens one at a time; attention computes all interactions at once — GPU-friendly.

quiz.q: Weight sharing in CNNs means:
choices: The same filter slides across the image — parameters don’t scale with image size
quiz.explain: One filter reused everywhere: parameter count depends on filter size, not image size.

cards.front: How do you frame a business goal as an ML problem?
cards.back: Translate the decision into prediction: what’s predicted, for whom, at what moment, with what latency, and how success is measured in business terms. The interview line: ‘framing is the highest-leverage ML skill — a perfect model for the wrong target is worthless.’

cards.front: Spark: partitions, shuffles, and skew — the interview version?
cards.back: Partitions are the parallelism unit; shuffles (repartitioning data across the network) are the expensive operation; skew (one giant key) kills parallelism. Fixes: salting skewed keys, broadcast joins for small tables, and repartitioning deliberately.

cards.front: What’s a feature store for?
cards.back: One place for feature definitions shared by training and serving: consistent computation (kills skew), point-in-time correctness for training, online/offline serving, and discovery/reuse. The interview line: ‘the feature store is where features become contracts.’

cards.front: How do you monitor models in production?
cards.back: Input drift (feature distributions vs training), prediction drift (output distribution shifts), performance decay (labels lag — use proxies), and data-quality checks on the pipeline. Triggers: retrain on schedule or on drift threshold — with a champion/challenger setup for safe rollout.

cards.front: Why ‘simple model first’ in ML system design?
cards.back: A linear model or heuristic sets the baseline, ships fast, and is debuggable — complexity must earn its keep against it. Most production wins come from features and data, not model architecture. The interview line: ‘I scale complexity with evidence, not enthusiasm.’

quiz.q: An ML system design that only covers the model is weak because:
choices: Production value lives in data, serving, and monitoring — the model is one piece
quiz.explain: Most ML failures are systems failures: skew, drift, latency — not the algorithm.

quiz.q: ‘Simple model first’ is justified because:
choices: It ships fast, debugs easily, and forces complexity to prove its value
quiz.explain: Baselines bound the problem: you learn whether the fancy model is worth its operational cost.

quiz.q: Prediction drift without label feedback is detected by:
choices: Comparing live prediction distributions to the training baseline — a leading indicator
quiz.explain: Labels arrive late; distribution shifts in inputs/outputs warn you first.

quiz.q: A feature store’s main reliability win is:
choices: Identical feature logic in training and serving — eliminating a whole class of skew
quiz.explain: One definition, two serving paths: the consistency guarantee is the product.

cards.front: How do you explain k-means in a coding interview?
cards.back: Alternate: assign points to nearest centroid, recompute centroids as means, repeat until stable. Know the caveats: k must be chosen (elbow/silhouette), sensitive to initialization (k-means++), assumes spherical clusters, and feature scaling matters.

cards.front: Gradient descent variants and failure modes?

cards.front: What does ‘ML coding under time pressure’ demand?
cards.back: Vectorized NumPy (no Python loops), shape discipline (assert shapes at each step — mismatches are the #1 time sink), deriving updates from definitions, and narrating as you code. The interview line: ‘I assert shapes the way others assert types.’

cards.front: Why narrate while writing ML code?
cards.back: The interviewer grades method: what each block computes, why this formulation, what could go wrong. Silent correct code scores less than narrated reasoning — the interview line: ‘my narration is the proof I’d write this the same way at 2am.’

cards.front: The interviewer asks you to go deep on 'Implementing k-means from scratch'. What answer structure makes you sound senior?
cards.back: Three beats: (1) one-sentence definition, (2) how it works mechanically, (3) when it fits and its key tradeoff — then stop and invite the follow-up. Structure is what separates a senior answer from a recitation.

choices: It exposes your reasoning to grading — and catches your own errors early
quiz.explain: Verbalized logic is checkable logic; most caught bugs are caught mid-sentence.

quiz.q: The fastest way to debug a shape mismatch in NumPy is:
choices: Printing/asserting shapes at each operation — the mismatch localizes instantly
quiz.explain: Shape errors are local: the first operation whose output shape surprises you is the bug.

quiz.q: Diverging loss (NaN/inf) in training most likely means:

quiz.q: k-means is sensitive to initialization because:
choices: Lloyd’s algorithm converges to local optima — different seeds give different clusterings
quiz.explain: The objective is non-convex; k-means++ seeding and multiple restarts mitigate bad local minima.

cards.front: How do you frame an ML problem and choose the metric?
cards.back: Translate the business decision into a prediction task (what, for whom, when), then pick the metric from the error costs — not from habit. The interview line: ‘the metric is the business objective, mathematized.’

cards.front: Why baseline before complexity in ML?
cards.back: A simple model sets the bar: every fancier model must beat it by enough to justify its cost. It also debugs the pipeline early — if the baseline fails, the problem is the data, not the model. The interview line: ‘complexity must earn its keep.’

cards.front: How do you run ML experiments with discipline?
cards.back: Track everything (params, data version, code hash, metrics) in an experiment tracker; change one thing at a time; ablate to assign credit. The interview line: ‘an untracked experiment is an anecdote.’

cards.front: What does real error analysis look like?
cards.back: Slice the errors: which subgroups/classes fail, look at actual examples (not just metrics), find patterns, and let the pattern choose the next move (more data? better features? label fixes?). The interview line: ‘metrics tell me I’m wrong; error analysis tells me why.’

cards.front: What’s a model card, and why write one?
cards.back: Documentation of intended use, training data, evaluation results, limitations, and ethical considerations — the model’s honest label. The interview line: ‘a model without a card is a black box I’m asking others to trust.’

quiz.q: The ‘what you’d do next’ close is strong because:
choices: It shows you see the work’s frontier — senior scope awareness
quiz.explain: Knowing the next step proves you owned the problem, not just the implementation.

quiz.q: A model card’s limitations section exists to:
choices: State where the model shouldn’t be trusted — preventing misuse
quiz.explain: Documented limits turn unknown unknowns into known ones for downstream users.

cards.front: Inner vs outer joins — drilled: what survives each?
cards.back: Inner: only matches. Left: all left rows. Right: all right rows. Full: everything. The drill: for ‘customers with no orders’ you need the LEFT and filter NULL — inner would silently drop the answer.

cards.front: How do you find ‘what’s missing’ in SQL?
cards.back: The anti-join: LEFT JOIN … WHERE right.key IS NULL, or NOT EXISTS (preferred — NULL-safe, unlike NOT IN). ‘Customers with no orders,’ ‘products never sold’ — this pattern is an interview staple.

cards.front: When do you use EXISTS vs a JOIN?
cards.back: EXISTS for semi-join questions (‘customers WITH orders’) — it stops at the first match and never fans out. JOIN when you need columns from the other table. The interview line: ‘EXISTS asks a yes/no question; JOIN brings back data.’

cards.front: EXISTS vs IN — the drill version?
cards.back: EXISTS: correlated, short-circuits, NULL-safe. IN: set membership, NULL-poisoned under NOT. The drill answer: ‘has at least one’ → EXISTS; ‘has none’ → NOT EXISTS; never NOT IN on nullable columns.

cards.front: How do you merge without fan-out disasters?
cards.back: Check key uniqueness on both sides first (one-to-many is fine; many-to-many explodes). Validate with row-count assertions before/after, and use validate='m:1' in pandas to enforce expectations loudly.

quiz.q: pd.merge(validate='m:1') is used to:
choices: Assert the merge keys have the expected uniqueness — failing loudly on fan-out
quiz.explain: Declaring expected cardinality turns silent row multiplication into a loud error.

quiz.q: NOT EXISTS is preferred over NOT IN when:
choices: The subquery column can be NULL — NOT IN then returns nothing
quiz.explain: Same NULL trap: NOT EXISTS has clean three-valued-logic semantics.

quiz.q: EXISTS is preferred over IN for ‘has at least one’ because:
choices: It short-circuits on first match and is NULL-safe
quiz.explain: Correlated EXISTS stops scanning at the first hit; IN materializes the whole set.

quiz.q: NOT IN is dangerous with NULLs because:
choices: A single NULL in the subquery makes the whole predicate UNKNOWN — zero rows returned
quiz.explain: NULL semantics: NOT IN with a NULL never evaluates true; NOT EXISTS doesn’t have this trap.

cards.front: How do you explain window functions in a SQL interview?
cards.back: ‘Calculations across rows without collapsing them’: ROW_NUMBER/RANK for top-N per group, LAG/LEAD for period-over-period, running totals with ordered frames. The key contrast: GROUP BY collapses rows; windows keep row detail and add context.

cards.front: How do you compute a running total?
cards.back: SUM(x) OVER (ORDER BY date ROWS UNBOUNDED PRECEDING) — the ordered frame accumulates. The interview details: frame clauses control the window (ROWS vs RANGE), and omitting ORDER BY makes the frame meaningless.

cards.front: What are NTILE and percent_rank for?
cards.back: NTILE(n): split ordered rows into n roughly-equal buckets (quartiles, deciles). percent_rank: relative standing from 0 to 1. The interview line: ‘NTILE buckets, percent_rank scores — both answer ‘where does this row stand?’’

cards.front: Windows vs GROUP BY — the drill distinction?
cards.back: GROUP BY collapses to one row per group. Windows compute across rows while keeping every row. The drill: ‘each employee with their department average’ — GROUP BY can’t do it alone; AVG() OVER (PARTITION BY dept) can.

cards.front: Top-N per group: the canonical pattern?
cards.back: ROW_NUMBER() OVER (PARTITION BY group ORDER BY metric DESC) in a CTE, then filter rn <= N in the outer query. Window functions can’t go in WHERE — the CTE-then-filter two-step is the pattern to recite.

quiz.q: Window functions can’t appear in WHERE because:
choices: They’re evaluated after WHERE in the logical query order — filter in an outer query
quiz.explain: Logical order: FROM → WHERE → GROUP BY → … → window functions → ORDER BY. Filter one level out.

quiz.q: ‘Each sale alongside its region’s total’ needs:
choices: A window: SUM(amount) OVER (PARTITION BY region) — detail preserved
quiz.explain: Windows add group context without collapsing: every row keeps its identity.

quiz.q: NTILE(4) over ordered salaries assigns:
quiz.explain: NTILE divides the ordered set into n buckets as evenly as possible.

quiz.q: In a window frame, ROWS vs RANGE differs in:
choices: ROWS counts physical rows; RANGE groups by peer values of ORDER BY
quiz.explain: RANGE with ties includes all peers — running totals over duplicate dates differ between the two.

scriptLabs.title: Month-over-month revenue growth (SQL)
scriptLabs.brief: The analytics bread-and-butter: aggregate to month grain in a CTE, then LAG for period-over-period growth. Grain first, window second — exactly as the module teaches.
scriptLabs.starter:
-- Columns: month, revenue, prev_revenue, mom_growth_pct
-- Table: orders(order_id, order_date, amount)
SELECT
scriptLabs.hint: Aggregate to month grain first in a CTE, then LAG over the ordered months. Guard division by zero with NULLIF.
scriptLabs.solution:
WITH monthly AS (
  SELECT DATE_TRUNC('month', order_date) AS month,
         SUM(amount) AS revenue
  FROM orders
  GROUP BY 1
)
SELECT month,
       revenue,
       LAG(revenue) OVER (ORDER BY month) AS prev_revenue,
       ROUND(100.0 * (revenue - LAG(revenue) OVER (ORDER BY month))
             / NULLIF(LAG(revenue) OVER (ORDER BY month), 0), 2) AS mom_growth_pct
FROM monthly
ORDER BY month;

from airflow import DAG
from airflow.operators.python import PythonOperator
from datetime import datetime, timedelta

def extract():
    print("extracting orders since last watermark")

def transform():
    print("cleaning, validating, conforming")

def load():

with DAG(
    dag_id="daily_orders",
    start_date=datetime(2026, 1, 1),
    schedule="@daily",
    catchup=False,
    default_args={

        "retry_delay": timedelta(minutes=5),

) as dag:

    t_transform = PythonOperator(task_id="transform", python_callable=transform)
    t_load = PythonOperator(task_id="load", python_callable=load)
    t_extract >> t_transform >> t_load

choices: UNION ALL keeps duplicates and skips the dedup sort — faster when dupes are fine
drills.explain: UNION’s implicit DISTINCT costs a sort; ALL avoids it when duplicates don’t matter.

drills.title: Statistics and Probability
choices: The procedure captures the true parameter in ~95% of repeated samples
drills.explain: Frequentist intervals describe the method’s long-run coverage, not a probability about this interval.

scenarios.title: SQL live-coding: top-N per group
scenarios.context: ‘For each department, show the top 3 earners.’ The interviewer is watching you think.

steps.prompt: Before writing anything, what do you clarify?

options.text: The grain and edge cases: one row per what, how to break salary ties, what ‘top’ means
options.why: Grain and tie-breaking decide between ROW_NUMBER, RANK, and DENSE_RANK — clarifying first picks the right tool.

options.text: Nothing — the question is clear enough
options.why: ‘Top 3’ with ties is genuinely ambiguous; assuming wastes the attempt when the interviewer meant distinct values.

options.text: Which SQL dialect the company uses
options.why: Dialect trivia can wait; the logic is dialect-independent and that’s what’s graded.

options.text: Whether you can use the internet
options.why: Live rounds test unaided reasoning; asking signals you can’t produce the pattern cold.

steps.prompt: Mid-query you blank on the window syntax. Strongest recovery?

options.text: Decompose aloud: ‘I need ranking inside each department — that’s ROW_NUMBER() OVER (PARTITION BY dept ORDER BY salary DESC) in a CTE, then filter rn <= 3 outside’
options.why: Decomposing into named steps and narrating the pattern shows the interviewer your reasoning even while the exact syntax returns.

options.text: Go silent until the syntax comes back
options.why: Silence is unscoreable; narrated decomposition is gradable and often jogs the memory.

options.text: Write a correlated subquery instead without saying why
options.why: Switching approaches silently looks like flailing; if you pivot, narrate the pivot.

options.text: Say ‘I don’t remember window functions’ and stop
options.why: Surrendering forfeits partial credit; the pattern’s logic is recoverable from first principles.

steps.prompt: The query runs. How do you verify it before declaring done?

options.text: Trace a tiny mental dataset through it: two departments, a tie, and check the output rows by hand
options.why: Mental-dataset verification catches grain, tie, and filter bugs — it’s the live-round equivalent of a test.

options.text: Declare victory — it parsed, so it’s right
options.why: Parsing isn’t correctness; untested SQL in an interview is a guess.

options.text: Ask the interviewer if it’s correct
options.why: Outsourcing verification forfeits the senior signal — checking your own work is the job.

options.text: Add more columns to look thorough
options.why: Extra output doesn’t verify correctness; it just adds surface for new bugs.

scenarios.title: Case round: conversion dropped 10%
scenarios.context: ‘Checkout conversion fell 10% week over week. Diagnose it.’ Whiteboard, 30 minutes.

options.text: Verify the data: instrumentation changes, pipeline delays, definition changes — rule out measurement artifacts
options.why: A large share of ‘metric moves’ are measurement artifacts; theorizing before verifying wastes the round.

options.text: Blame the latest product release
options.why: The newest change is a hypothesis, not a conclusion — and it skips the data-quality check entirely.

options.text: Propose three product hypotheses immediately
options.why: Hypotheses before verification build on possibly-broken data; order matters and it’s graded.

options.text: Ask for a month of raw data to explore
options.why: Boiling the ocean burns the clock; structured diagnosis beats undirected exploration.

steps.prompt: Data checks out — the drop is real. Next?

options.text: Segment: which slice moved (device, channel, cohort, geography)? Then rank hypotheses per segment
options.why: Segmentation localizes the cause; hypotheses ranked per segment turn one mystery into testable pieces.

options.text: Compute the overall average again more carefully
options.why: Recomputing the aggregate you already trust adds nothing; the answer is in the segments.

options.text: Recommend reverting the last release
options.why: Recommending action before localizing the cause is guessing with consequences.

options.text: Build a predictive model of conversion
options.why: Modeling before diagnosing answers a different question — and takes far longer than the round allows.

steps.prompt: Mobile web conversion collapsed; desktop is flat. How do you confirm the mechanism?

options.text: Funnel-by-step on mobile web plus the ‘did the denominator change’ check (traffic mix vs true rate drop)
options.why: The diagnostic query set: localize the funnel step, then separate mix effects from real rate changes — the complete analyst move.

options.text: Declare ‘mobile is broken’ and recommend a rewrite
options.why: A segment-level finding isn’t a mechanism; the funnel step and denominator check are still missing.

options.text: Average mobile and desktop together for the report
options.why: Re-aggregating destroys the segmentation insight you just earned.

options.text: Wait for more data next week
options.why: Deferring a diagnosable problem signals you can’t drive to an answer under time pressure.

scenarios.title: Behavioral: ‘Tell me about a failed analysis’
scenarios.context: The data-science behavioral round. They want the failed-analysis story — told with ownership.

steps.prompt: How do you frame the failure?

options.text: Own it early: what you concluded, why it was wrong, and what the miss cost — then the fix
options.why: Early ownership establishes credibility; the story’s value is in what changed, which needs the honest setup.

options.text: Frame it as actually a success — ‘it taught the team a lot’
options.why: Reframing failure as success dodges the question; interviewers asked for a failure.

options.text: Blame the data quality — it wasn’t your fault
options.why: Data problems are the analyst’s jurisdiction; blaming them fails the ownership test.

options.text: Pick a trivial failure with no stakes
options.why: Stakes-free stories reveal nothing about judgment; pick one where the miss mattered.

options.text: A concrete process change: the validation step you added (e.g. always check the denominator, always segment first)
options.why: A specific changed practice — with evidence it caught something later — turns failure into growth.

options.text: ‘I’m more careful now’
options.why: Vague resolutions aren’t resolutions; interviewers score the mechanism, not the sentiment.

options.text: Nothing — it was a one-off
options.why: ‘One-off’ claims end the learning arc; every real miss has a systemic lesson.

options.text: You switched teams
options.why: Changing scenery isn’t a lesson; it reads as avoidance.

options.text: The lesson as practice: ‘that miss is why I now verify data quality before theorizing — it’s caught two artifacts since’
options.why: A lesson with evidence it stuck is the strongest possible close for a failure story.

options.text: Apologize for the failure again
options.why: Repeated apologies re-center shame instead of growth; one ownership statement suffices.

options.text: Emphasize how bad you felt
options.why: Feelings aren’t the deliverable; the changed practice is.

options.text: Pivot to a success story
options.why: Pivoting away signals discomfort with the failure — land the lesson instead.

choices: Some rows have NULL email — COUNT(column) skips NULLs
mockTasks.explain: COUNT(column) excludes NULLs; COUNT(*) counts every row regardless.

mockTasks.q: Diverging loss (NaN/inf) in training most likely means:
choices: Learning rate too large for the loss curvature
mockTasks.explain: Overshooting the minimum repeatedly: reduce lr (or add scheduling/clipping) first.

mockTasks.q: COUNT(DISTINCT customer_id) vs COUNT(*) differ when:
choices: Rows aren’t unique per customer — COUNT(*) counts rows, COUNT(DISTINCT) counts customers
mockTasks.explain: Grain discipline: know what one row represents before choosing the aggregate.

choices: Using normal-based confidence intervals on sample means from non-normal data (with enough samples)
mockTasks.explain: Sample means converge to normal as n grows — the foundation of classical inference on means.

choices: HAVING — it filters groups after aggregation
mockTasks.explain: WHERE filters rows pre-aggregation; HAVING filters the grouped results.

mockTasks.q: Minimizing MSE is equivalent to MLE under:
mockTasks.explain: The Gaussian likelihood’s log is the squared error (up to constants) — same optimum.

mockTasks.q: Pure transform functions are testable because:
choices: Determinism: no mocks needed, every case is an input/output pair
mockTasks.explain: Purity removes the test setup tax; the function’s contract is its signature.

choices: That the notebook has no hidden out-of-order state — true top-to-bottom reproducibility
mockTasks.explain: Out-of-order execution hides state dependencies; a clean rerun proves the narrative is real.

mockTasks.q: The clearest signal to move from spreadsheet to SQL/Python is:
choices: Manual steps that must be repeated reliably — reproducibility and scale
mockTasks.explain: Repetition + scale + auditability: the point where manual stops being trustworthy.

mockTasks.q: Training loss falling while validation loss rises means:
choices: Overfitting — the model memorizes training noise
mockTasks.explain: The divergence point is where generalization ends; early stopping lives there.

mockTasks.q: Window functions can’t appear in WHERE because:
choices: They’re evaluated after WHERE in the logical query order — filter in an outer query
mockTasks.explain: Logical order: FROM → WHERE → GROUP BY → … → window functions → ORDER BY. Filter one level out.

mockTasks.q: df['x'].apply(f) vs a vectorized equivalent: the difference is:
choices: apply still loops in Python; vectorized ops execute in compiled C — often 10-100x faster
mockTasks.explain: apply is a disguised Python loop; true vectorization pushes the loop into C.

mockTasks.q: Building features before the train/test split risks:
choices: Leakage — statistics from the test set contaminating training features
mockTasks.explain: Any transform that learns from data must be fit on train only, or evaluation is fiction.

mockTasks.q: Formula-based cleaning beats manual edits because:
choices: It’s auditable and re-runnable — manual edits can’t be verified or repeated
mockTasks.explain: Repeatability is the difference between analysis and anecdote.

choices: Randomly zeroes activations so the network can’t rely on any single unit — an implicit ensemble
mockTasks.explain: Forcing redundancy across units prevents co-adaptation; at inference the full network is used (scaled).

mockTasks.q: ‘Each sale alongside its region’s total’ needs:
choices: A window: SUM(amount) OVER (PARTITION BY region) — detail preserved
mockTasks.explain: Windows add group context without collapsing: every row keeps its identity.

blocks.body: **ROW_NUMBER()**: unique 1,2,3. **RANK()**: 1,2,2,4 (gaps). **DENSE_RANK()**: 1,2,2,3 (no gaps). ‘Top 3 distinct’ → DENSE_RANK; ‘exactly 3 rows’ → ROW_NUMBER.
**LAG/LEAD(col) OVER (ORDER BY t)**: previous/next row — period-over-period. **FIRST_VALUE/LAST_VALUE**: frame edges.
Running total: `SUM(x) OVER (ORDER BY d ROWS UNBOUNDED PRECEDING)`. **ROWS** = physical rows; **RANGE** = peer values.
CTE: `ROW_NUMBER() OVER (PARTITION BY g ORDER BY m DESC) AS rn` → outer query `WHERE rn <= N`. Windows can’t go in WHERE — filter one level out.
Randomization unit → primary metric + guardrails → MDE from business value → sample size & runtime from power (80%) → **pre-registered analysis plan**.

**Peeking**: every look compounds false positives — pre-commit the runtime. **Multiple testing**: more metrics, more false wins — correct or prioritize. **Ignoring SUTVA**: network effects break randomization.
CI around the estimate (not just the point), guardrails checked, segment heterogeneity examined. A win with regressed guardrails is a tradeoff, not a victory.
Can’t randomize cleanly, tiny samples, months-long effects, unethical, or obvious from data — then quasi-experiments or ship-with-monitoring.
`groupby(...).agg(...)` for summaries; `.transform(...)` to broadcast back to rows (same shape out); `.filter(...)` on group properties.
Check key uniqueness first; `validate='m:1'` fails loudly on fan-out. `indicator=True` shows merge provenance.
Boolean masks, `np.where`, string methods — never `iterrows`. 10–100x faster and shorter. `apply` is a disguised Python loop.
`chunksize` + incremental aggregation, `usecols`, dtype downcasting. Never assume the data fits in memory.
`pd.to_datetime`, timezone-aware, store UTC. DST makes naive arithmetic ambiguous.
Full vs incremental (watermark: updated_at/CDC). Incremental needs late-arrival handling — it’s an optimization with a correctness contract.
DAGs as code, sensors for external state, retries with backoff for transient failure, SLA + alerting for the on-call reality.
**Idempotent** stages (reruns safe) · partition-scoped backfills · DQ gates at layer boundaries (freshness, volume, schema, distribution) · fail or quarantine, never silently pass bad data.
Grain first, then star schema; SCD Type 2 when history matters; bronze → silver → gold with contracts between layers; dbt tests on every model.

answerBank.q: Window functions vs GROUP BY — when do you use each?
answerBank.a: GROUP BY collapses rows to one per group — use it for pure aggregates. Window functions compute across rows while keeping every row — ‘each employee alongside their department average’ needs AVG() OVER (PARTITION BY dept). The rule: if the question wants detail plus context, it’s a window; if it wants one row per group, it’s GROUP BY.

answerBank.q: How do you design an A/B test?
answerBank.a: Randomization unit, primary metric plus guardrail metrics, MDE from business value, sample size and runtime from a power calculation — and a pre-registered analysis plan before the first user is enrolled. During the run: no peeking (pre-commit the stopping rule), and at read-out I check the confidence interval, guardrails, and segment heterogeneity, not just the point estimate.

answerBank.q: The metric moved — walk me through your diagnosis.
answerBank.a: First, verify the data: instrumentation changes, pipeline delays, definition changes — rule out measurement artifacts. Then segment to find which slice moved, form ranked hypotheses per segment, and test with the diagnostic query set: funnel by segment, cohort check, and the ‘did the denominator change’ query. Only then do I recommend. Data-quality before storytelling — the order is what’s graded.

answerBank.q: Batch vs streaming — how do you choose?
answerBank.a: By latency need versus cost and complexity: batch is simpler, cheaper, and easier to get exactly right — the default. Streaming earns its keep when decisions need minutes, not hours. I name the costs honestly: watermarks and late data, exactly-once complexity, and operational burden. Kappa (one streaming pipeline with log replay) unless I can name why batch is required.

answerBank.q: How do you handle training/serving skew?
answerBank.a: Skew means features at serving time differ systematically from training — usually different code paths computing them. Prevention: shared feature logic via a feature store, point-in-time correctness for training data. Detection: log serving features and monitor input/prediction distributions against the training baseline, with retraining triggers on drift. Same model, different data is a silent failure — so I make the data pipeline the tested contract.

Every model balances two errors: bias is the model being too simple to capture reality (underfitting — consistently wrong), variance is it being too sensitive to the specific data it saw (overfitting — great on past data, bad on new). More data tames variance; the right model complexity tames bias. We pick the sweet spot with validation — testing on data the model hasn’t seen.

answerBank.q: Tell me about a failed analysis.
answerBank.a: STAR with ownership: what I concluded, why it was wrong, and what the miss cost — stated early and plainly. Then the concrete process change it produced (e.g. always verifying data quality before theorizing, always checking the denominator), with evidence the change caught something later. The failure is the setup; the changed practice with proof is the point.
